pairs.rationale: The Psalm's invitation to sit at the Lord's right hand corresponds to Hebrews' right-hand enthronement language. Hebrews identifies the seated figure as our high priest and adds the heavenly throne of the Majesty; the selected Psalm sentence does not itself name the priestly office.

The source calls the sanctuary the true tent pitched by the Lord rather than a human. The later passage describes Christ's greater and more perfect tent as not made by hands and not of this creation, preserving its distinct descriptive wording.

The earlier statement likewise defines every high priest's appointment in terms of offering gifts and sacrifices, explicitly for sins. The source uses that function to infer that this One also must have something to offer.

The earlier tribal argument identifies the Lord with Judah rather than the tribe serving at the altar. This provides the legal-priesthood context for the source's earthly-priesthood counterfactual and its reference to lawful gift offerers.

Exodus supplies the command to make according to the pattern shown on the mountain. Exodus prints make them, while Hebrews prints make everything and uses the instruction to explain the copy-and-shadow service.

Both passages name a better covenant in connection with Jesus' priestly role. The source calls Him mediator and mentions better promises; the earlier passage calls Him guarantor. These related titles are retained as distinct.

The source argues that seeking a second covenant implies a fault in the first. After the intervening new-covenant quotation, the target draws the related conclusion that calling it new makes the first old and aging.

Jeremiah 38:31 promises a new covenant with the houses of Israel and Judah. Hebrews prints Look and conclude where Jeremiah prints Behold and make, and adds the introductory finding-fault clause before the quotation.

Both passages contrast the promised covenant with the fathers' exodus covenant and say they did not remain in it and the Lord disregarded them. Their hand-taking and leading-out phrases differ slightly; the supplied Greek-based Jeremiah wording is preserved.

Jeremiah 38:33 supplies the promised laws within and written on hearts, followed by God-and-people belonging. Both retain My laws in the plural; Hebrews prints mind and inscribe where Jeremiah prints understanding and write.

The first part of Jeremiah 38:34 supplies the fellow-citizen-and-brother teaching contrast and knowledge of the Lord from least to greatest. The target also contains the mercy-and-sins sentence, which Hebrews places in its following verse.

The closing part of Jeremiah 38:34 supplies mercy and sins remembered no more. Hebrews prints wrongdoings where Jeremiah prints injustices; Jeremiah's same verse also contains the preceding knowledge-of-the-Lord promise.

The source explicitly reasons from the word new in the earlier new-covenant declaration. Linking that precise wording makes the new-versus-old inference visible without assigning an external date to the predicted disappearance.

distinctions: Psalm 109 native numbering; right-hand language is linked without treating the selected Psalm sentence as naming the high-priest office.
Jeremiah 38:31-34, not conventional Hebrew chapter 31; laws plural and mind/understanding, inscribe/write, wrongdoings/injustices differences kept.
Exodus 25:40 them and Hebrews everything; guarantor and mediator remain distinct.
The new/old inference is internal textual reasoning, without importing a historical disappearance date.
